title: The prime-to-characteristic local Galois calculation
statement:
Let $R$ be an excellent discrete valuation ring [def-exc-excellent-ring, def-sc-discrete-valuation-ring] which is
strictly henselian [def-weil-pbc-henselian-terminology],
with algebraically closed residue field of characteristic $p>0$.
Put $F=\operatorname{Frac}(R)$, let $G=\operatorname{Gal}(F^{\rm sep}/F)$,
and fix a prime $\ell\neq p$. If $A$ is a finite ring killed by a power
of $\ell$, then for every
discrete continuous
$A[G]$-module $M$, with cohomology as in [def-exc-continuous-cohomology], one has

$$
H^q(G,M)=0\quad(q>1).
$$

If $M$ is finite, then $H^0(G,M)$ and $H^1(G,M)$ are finite.

proof.text: The strictly henselian ring in the statement is henselian by [def-weil-pbc-henselian-terminology]. Apply [lem-exc-henselian-dvr-tame-sequence] to this excellent DVR $R$ with its algebraically closed residue field of characteristic $p>0$ and fraction field $F$. Fix the continuous surjection $\theta:G\to T=\prod_{r\neq p}(\mathbf Z_r,+)$ supplied by that lemma, with closed normal pro-$p$ kernel $P$ and topological quotient $G/P\cong T$.

source.place: Proof, first two paragraphs; finite and infinite ramification calculation made a structural dependency

proof.text:
Let $B=\prod_{r
eq p,\ell}\mathbf Z_r$, and let $H=\ker(\operatorname{pr}_{\ell}\circ	heta)$, a closed normal subgroup of $G$. Then $H/P\cong B$ and $G/H\cong(\mathbf Z_\ell,+)$ as topological groups. For a finite continuous quotient $Q$ of $H$, the image of $P$ is a finite continuous quotient of $P$, hence a $p$-group by Step 1. The quotient of $Q$ by this image is a finite continuous quotient of $B$. Its kernel is open, so it contains a basic open subgroup restricting only finitely many coordinates to $r^{n_r}\mathbf Z_r$; consequently this quotient is a quotient of a finite product of groups $\mathbf Z/r^{n_r}\mathbf Z$ with $r
eq\ell$. Its order is prime to $\ell$. The order formula for a finite group and a normal subgroup now shows $\ell
mid |Q|$. The topological quotient identifications follow from the continuous surjections between compact Hausdorff groups.

source.place: Proof, second paragraph, construction of H and its finite quotients

proof.text: Write $\mathcal C_G$ and $\mathcal C_{G/H}$ for the categories in [lem-exc-discrete-modules-abelian]. Choose $s\geq0$ with $\ell^s A=0$. Define $V:\mathcal C_G\to\mathcal C_{G/H}$ by $V(N)=N^H$ with the induced action and restriction on morphisms. Restrictions of sums of morphisms are sums, so $V$ is additive. Normality of $H$ makes $N^H$ stable under $G$; its stabilizers in $G/H$ are open because their preimages are the open stabilizers in $G$ of its elements. Kernels are preserved: an element of the kernel is $H$-fixed exactly when it belongs to the kernel of the restricted map. For a surjection $N\to N'$ and $y\in(N')^H$, choose a lift $x\in N$. The $H$-orbit of $x$ is finite because its stabilizer is open in the compact group $H$. The $A$-span $L$ of this orbit is a finite, $H$-stable module, since $A$ is finite. Intersect the stabilizers of all elements of $L$ to obtain an open normal subgroup $U\triangleleft H$ acting trivially on $L$. Thus $Q=H/U$ acts on $L$, and Step 2 gives $\ell\nmid |Q|$. Choose integers $a,b$ with $a|Q|+b\ell^s=1$, where $\ell^sA=0$. The element $x_0=a\sum_{q\in Q}qx$ is independent of coset representatives, is fixed by $H$, and maps to $a|Q|y=y$. This proves surjectivity on fixed elements. Exactness on underlying modules is exactness in both categories by the cited node, so $V$ is exact.

source.place: Proof, third paragraph, the averaging argument with its finite quotient and inverse of the group order written out

proof.text: Let $\operatorname{Inf}:\mathcal C_{G/H}\to\mathcal C_G$ be inflation along $G\to G/H$: it keeps the underlying $A$-module and precomposes the action. The inverse image of an open stabilizer is open, so inflation is defined. It preserves monomorphisms, since these are underlying injections by [lem-exc-discrete-modules-abelian]. A $G$-equivariant map $\operatorname{Inf}(X)\to N$ has image in $N^H$, and factoring through this submodule gives exactly a $(G/H)$-equivariant map $X\to V(N)$; the two operations are inverse. To check that $V(I)$ is injective when $I$ is injective, take a monomorphism $X\hookrightarrow Y$ and a map $X\to V(I)$. The corresponding map $\operatorname{Inf}(X)\to I$ extends to $\operatorname{Inf}(Y)\to I$ by the definition of injectivity in [def-sp-injective-resolutions]. Factoring the extension through $V(I)$ extends the original map. This proves that $V(I)$ is injective.

source.place: Proof, third paragraph, exact inflation and preservation of injectives by the fixed-submodule functor

proof.text: Choose an injective resolution $M\to I^\bullet$ in $\mathcal C_G$, which exists by [lem-exc-discrete-modules-abelian]. Step 3 makes $M^H\to V(I^\bullet)$ exact, and Step 4 makes every $V(I^n)$ injective in $\mathcal C_{G/H}$; thus it is an injective resolution there. For each term one has $(I^n)^G=((I^n)^H)^{G/H}$ as the very same submodule of $I^n$, and the differentials on these submodules are the same restrictions. By the injective-resolution definition of continuous cohomology in [def-exc-continuous-cohomology] and of right derived functors in [def-sp-left-exact-additive], this single complex therefore computes both $H^q(G,M)$ and $H^q(G/H,M^H)$. Identifying $G/H$ with $\mathbf Z_\ell$ from Step 2 just relabels the action through the topological group isomorphism: the equivariant maps and fixed submodules are identical under that relabelling. Consequently $H^q(G,M)\cong H^q(\mathbf Z_\ell,M^H)$ for every $q\geq0$.

source.place: Proof, third paragraph, comparison by the same injective-resolution complex

proof.text: The submodule $M^H$ is a discrete continuous $A[\mathbf Z_\ell]$-module by Step 3 and the topological identification of Step 2, and $\ell^sM^H=0$ because $\ell^sA=0$. Apply [lem-exc-procyclic-two-term] with the prime $\ell$, the finite ring $A$, and this module, using the generator $1\in\mathbf Z_\ell$. Its two-term complex $[M^H\xrightarrow{\tau-1}M^H]$ computes the right-hand cohomology of Step 5. The complex is zero outside degrees zero and one, so its cohomology vanishes in every degree $q>1$. Its degree-zero cohomology is $\ker(\tau-1)$ and its degree-one cohomology is $M^H/(\tau-1)M^H$. If $M$ is finite, its submodule $M^H$ is finite, and these kernel and quotient sets are finite. The identification in Step 5 proves both finiteness clauses and the required vanishing for $G$.

source.place: Proof, final two paragraphs, procyclic calculation and finiteness
